record.paper_title: Open Problems in Universal Induction & Intelligence
record.original_question: How should confirmation theory resolve the black raven paradox, namely the tension between the claim that observing black ravens confirms the hypothesis that all ravens are black, the logical equivalence of 'all ravens are black' with 'all non-black things are non-ravens', and the apparently absurd conclusion that observing a white sock therefore confirms that all ravens are black?

evidence.quote: b) The black raven paradox by Carl Gustav Hempel goes as follows [Res01, Ch.11.4]: Observing Black Ravens confirms the hypothesis H that all ravens are black. In general, (i) hypothesis R→B is confirmed by R-instances with property B. Formally substituting R❀¬B and B❀¬R leads to (ii) hypothesis ¬B→¬R is confirmed by ¬B-instances with property ¬R. But (iii) since R→B and ¬B → ¬R are logically equivalent, R→B must also be confirmed by ¬B-instance with property ¬R. Hence by (i), observing Black Ravens confirms Hypothesis H, so by (iii), observing White Socks also confirms that all Ravens are Black, since White Socks are non-Ravens which are non-Black. But this conclusion is absurd.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Hempel's raven paradox arises from three apparently plausible principles in confirmation theory:

(i) (Nicod's criterion) For predicates R and B, the universal hypothesis "for all x, R(x) → B(x)" is confirmed by observing an instance a satisfying R(a) ∧ B(a).

(ii) Applying (i) with R replaced by ¬B and B replaced by ¬R: the hypothesis "for all x, ¬B(x) → ¬R(x)" is confirmed by observing an instance a satisfying ¬B(a) ∧ ¬R(a).

(iii) (Equivalence condition) If two hypotheses are logically equivalent, then any observation that confirms one confirms the other. Since "∀x (R(x) → B(x))" and "∀x (¬B(x) → ¬R(x))" are logically equivalent, observations of the form ¬B(a) ∧ ¬R(a) confirm "all R are B" as well.

Taking R(x) = "x is a raven" and B(x) = "x is black", (iii) yields the conclusion that observing a white sock (a non-black non-raven) confirms the hypothesis that all ravens are black, which appears absurd.

Problem: Provide a formal theory of confirmation — specifying a precise quantitative or qualitative confirmation relation between evidence and hypotheses — that (a) clearly identifies which of the principles (i)–(iii) must be modified or restricted, (b) accounts for the intuition that observing black ravens provides substantially more confirmation of "all ravens are black" than observing white socks does (or explains rigorously why such a difference of degree is or is not warranted), and (c) does so in a way that is consistent across reformulations of the hypothesis under logical equivalence and choice of predicates.
artifact.status_search_result: The raven paradox remains a debated foundational problem in confirmation theory and inductive logic. While Bayesian analyses (Good, Hosiasson-Lindenbaum, Fitelson & Hawthorne, Vranas, and others) offer partial resolutions showing that white socks do confirm the hypothesis but only to a tiny degree under certain priors, there is no universally accepted resolution; competing approaches differ on which of Nicod's criterion, the equivalence condition, or background assumptions to revise. The problem is typically classified as open / unresolved in the philosophy of science and inductive logic literature.

status_evidence.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Confirmation
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses Hempel's raven paradox and the variety of Bayesian and non-Bayesian responses, noting continued disagreement about the correct resolution.
status_evidence.claim: The raven paradox remains an unresolved problem with multiple competing proposed resolutions.

status_evidence.title: Fitelson & Hawthorne, 'How Bayesian Confirmation Theory Handles the Paradox of the Ravens'
status_evidence.snippet: Bayesian frameworks show black ravens generally confirm the hypothesis more strongly than non-black non-ravens, but the result depends on substantive probabilistic assumptions.
status_evidence.claim: Partial Bayesian resolutions exist but rely on contested assumptions; no consensus solution.
